redcap_row.comments_v2: Following EMS handoff ending at 01:01, roles were assigned and chest compressions started at 01:20. The team leader immediately recognized PEA as a non-shockable rhythm (01:33), ordered Epinephrine #1 (administered at 01:43), and secured an LMA airway (01:50). Lung auscultation confirmed bilateral breath sounds at 03:25. At the first pulse check (03:47-03:56), PEA persisted and compressions resumed promptly. Epinephrine #2 was given at 04:04 (slightly early, ~2m20s after dose #1). H's and T's were thoroughly discussed (hypoxia, PE/thrombosis, electrolyte derangements, acidosis, hypoglycemia checked at 04:19). However, empirically treating severe hypovolemia with IV fluids during arrest was missed until after ROSC was achieved at 06:08 (fluids ordered at 06:35).
redcap_row.feedback_narrative_v2: Strong ACLS algorithm adherence for PEA arrest: rapid role assignment after handoff, immediate recognition of non-shockable PEA at 01:33, prompt first dose of Epinephrine at 01:43, and minimal peri-pause interruption during the 03:47 pulse check. Good collaborative brainstorming of H's and T's starting at 02:20 and point-of-care glucose check at 04:11. Opportunities for improvement: (1) Epinephrine #2 was given at 04:04, only ~2 minutes and 20 seconds after the first dose (target interval is 3-5 minutes); (2) Given the 48-hour history of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and poor PO intake, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation should be initiated during the PEA arrest rather than waiting until post-ROSC (06:35); (3) Ensure compressors switch every 2 minutes during pulse checks to prevent fatigue.
redcap_row.general_comments_v2: The team leader maintained a calm, organized overview and encouraged input from all team members. Closed-loop communication was present for medication administration and lung sound checks, though the compressor worked continuously from 01:20 to 06:08 without rotating — Specifically, role assignment was established at @01:02 (utt_002) and collaborative H's & T's input was solicited at @02:53 (utt_008), with verbal readback on Epinephrine #1 (@01:41–01:48) and bilateral breath sounds (@03:11–03:18). However, at @05:51 (utt_019), Sodium Bicarbonate was suggested ('We could do an amp of sodium bicarbonate') without a directed order to MED_RN or verbal administration readback (total_bicarb_v2 = 0), and a single compressor (CLIN-2) performed chest compressions continuously for 4m 48s (@01:20–06:08) without switching at the @03:49 rhythm check.

utterances.text: I'm EMS, I'm also your facilitator. Some disbelief will be suspended. When I ask you guys to intubate with the LMA, just bag or verbalize bagging, when you're giving meds, verbalize the meds. So this woman is a 57-year-old woman who has emphysema and is on oxygen at home. Her family states that the patient has been ill with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for several days. In the past 48 hours, she has been unable to eat or drink anything. Today she had more trouble breathing than usual and her breathing has gradually worsened. She was found by EMS unresponsive and cyanotic at home. We found her in a hospital-type bed and she appeared to be non-responsive. We started CPR and we placed an IV. Her initial vitals, she had a heart rate of 116, respiratory rate of 0, there was no pulse, no oxygen, and her heart rhythm was sinus tachycardia with PEA. Please assign yourself roles and begin.
Do you like compressions or airway? Okay, you can do compressions, I'll do airway. Meds. I can be the provider. Alright, so compressions.

Start compressions. So we knew she was in PEA when she came in. We don't have an airway, so if we want to get an airway. She's currently in PEA still, so we can't shock. We need to push 1 of epinephrine while we're getting the airway.
So I'm going to give meds, 1 milligram of epinephrine.
Okay, so 1 of epinephrine is given, we have our airway, we're currently bagging, we're doing CPR. Airway's in.

So we know that she was found unresponsive, she has a history of emphysema. She wears oxygen at home we know about. As far as like H's and T's, she could be hypoxic, she could have any type of clot or thrombus with her emphysema breathing history, PE. Does she have a cardiac history?
And she was having diarrhea before.
Right, so that makes sense for electrolyte derangements. We know it's PEA, it's probably we'll say 2 minutes, we can do a pulse check, we already pushed 1 of epinephrine. Any other suggestions?
If we could listen to lung sounds to confirm placement.
Listening... You hear bilateral breath sounds.
We can say it's about 2 minutes, so let's do a pulse check and see where rhythm's at. Does she have a pulse?
You do not feel a pulse.
Okay, so continue compressions, she's still in PEA. We can give another push of epinephrine if it's been 2 minutes.
Gave epinephrine.
Can we get a point-of-care glucose? Do we have labs back?
We don't have labs back, but your point-of-care glucose is within normal range.
We could do like a CBC, CMP, I would do a troponin, VBG and lactate, or just do an ABG and just see what her oxygen status was before, do a D-dimer. Is family here?
No, family is not here.
We could do an amp of sodium bicarbonate, I'm sure she's got some acidosis going on. It's about 2 minutes, we can check a pulse again. Do we have a pulse?
You guys have a pulse. So now her repeat vitals are she is tachycardic to 110, blood pressure is 95 over 77, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 is 94, and her PCO2 is 40.
Do we know what rhythm she's in? Normal sinus. Do we want to give fluids? She's dehydrated most likely.
Can we consult someone like pulm, cardiology should be consulted. We're still waiting for blood work, I would get an EKG now or CT, chest x-ray to confirm the ET tube and everything.
Alright guys, this ends your sim. Thank you.

  [05:51 / 351.0s–367.0s] TEAM_LEADER [DIRECTIVE] -> pulse_check: "We could do an amp of sodium bicarbonate, I'm sure she's got some acidosis going on. It's about 2 minutes, we can check a pulse again. Do we have a pulse?"
  [06:08 / 368.0s–387.0s] OTHER -> rosc_detected: "You guys have a pulse. So now her repeat vitals are she is tachycardic to 110, blood pressure is 95 over 77, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 is 94, and her PCO2 is 40."
  [06:29 / 389.0s–398.0s] TEAM_LEADER -> medication_administration: "Do we know what rhythm she's in? Normal sinus. Do we want to give fluids? She's dehydrated most likely."
  [07:04 / 424.0s–442.0s] TEAM_LEADER: "Can we consult someone like pulm, cardiology should be consulted. We're still waiting for blood work, I would get an EKG now or CT, chest x-ray to confirm the ET tube and everything."
  [07:22 / 442.5s–446.0s] OTHER: "Alright guys, this ends your sim. Thank you."

engine_team_review.team_narrative: The team leader maintained a calm, organized overview and encouraged input from all team members. Closed-loop communication was present for medication administration and lung sound checks, though the compressor worked continuously from 01:20 to 06:08 without rotating — Specifically, role assignment was established at @01:02 (utt_002) and collaborative H's & T's input was solicited at @02:53 (utt_008), with verbal readback on Epinephrine #1 (@01:41–01:48) and bilateral breath sounds (@03:11–03:18). However, at @05:51 (utt_019), Sodium Bicarbonate was suggested ('We could do an amp of sodium bicarbonate') without a directed order to MED_RN or verbal administration readback (total_bicarb_v2 = 0), and a single compressor (CLIN-2) performed chest compressions continuously for 4m 48s (@01:20–06:08) without switching at the @03:49 rhythm check.
engine_team_review.technical_narrative: Following EMS handoff ending at 01:01, roles were assigned and chest compressions started at 01:20. The team leader immediately recognized PEA as a non-shockable rhythm (01:33), ordered Epinephrine #1 (administered at 01:43), and secured an LMA airway (01:50). Lung auscultation confirmed bilateral breath sounds at 03:25. At the first pulse check (03:47-03:56), PEA persisted and compressions resumed promptly. Epinephrine #2 was given at 04:04 (slightly early, ~2m20s after dose #1). H's and T's were thoroughly discussed (hypoxia, PE/thrombosis, electrolyte derangements, acidosis, hypoglycemia checked at 04:19). However, empirically treating severe hypovolemia with IV fluids during arrest was missed until after ROSC was achieved at 06:08 (fluids ordered at 06:35).
engine_team_review.feedback_narrative: Strong ACLS algorithm adherence for PEA arrest: rapid role assignment after handoff, immediate recognition of non-shockable PEA at 01:33, prompt first dose of Epinephrine at 01:43, and minimal peri-pause interruption during the 03:47 pulse check. Good collaborative brainstorming of H's and T's starting at 02:20 and point-of-care glucose check at 04:11. Opportunities for improvement: (1) Epinephrine #2 was given at 04:04, only ~2 minutes and 20 seconds after the first dose (target interval is 3-5 minutes); (2) Given the 48-hour history of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and poor PO intake, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation should be initiated during the PEA arrest rather than waiting until post-ROSC (06:35); (3) Ensure compressors switch every 2 minutes during pulse checks to prevent fatigue.

done_well.title: Immediate Bedside Role Assignment & Calm, Organized Command
done_well.detail: Within 1 second of EMS handoff completion (@01:01), the Team Leader explicitly assigned Compressor, Airway, Medication RN, and Leader roles before initiating tasks, maintaining calm situational oversight throughout the code.
done_well.evidence_quote: [01:02 / 62.0s] TEAM_LEADER [DIRECTIVE]: "Do you like compressions or airway? Okay, you can do compressions, I'll do airway. Meds. I can be the provider. Alright, so compressions."
done_well.human_concordance: Matches Human TEAM Review: "they had clear defined roles and were calm and organized"

done_well.title: High Chest Compression Fraction (97.6% CCF) & Zero Prolonged Pauses (>10s)
done_well.detail: Chest compressions started at @01:20 (11s after simulation start at @01:09) and sustained a 97.6% CCF (ACLS target ≥80%). Both pulse/rhythm checks were tightly bounded under the 10-second ACLS limit (6.0s at @03:49–03:55 and 3.5s at @06:05–06:08).
done_well.modality: S1 Optical Flow (15 FPS) + Gemini P1 Vision
done_well.evidence_quote: [01:20 / 80.0s] Provider in black scrubs (CLIN-2) initiates sternal compressions; S1 optical-flow velocity track confirms 359.0s active CPR / 368.0s code window (Pause #1 = 6.0s @03:49, Pause #2 = 3.5s @06:05).
done_well.human_concordance: Verified within 0.0s of Human Golden Timestamp (time_compressions = 01:20)

done_well.title: Immediate Non-Shockable PEA Recognition & Prompt Epinephrine #1 with Readback
done_well.detail: Leader correctly verbalized that Sinus Tachycardia PEA is non-shockable (0 inappropriate shocks), ordered 1 mg IV Epinephrine at @01:20 while simultaneous LMA airway placement proceeded (@01:50), received verbal announcement from MED_RN at @01:41, and closed the loop at @01:48.
done_well.evidence_quote: [01:20] TEAM_LEADER: "She's currently in PEA still, so we can't shock. We need to push 1 of epinephrine" → [01:41] MED_RN: "So I'm going to give meds, 1 milligram of epinephrine" → [01:48] TEAM_LEADER: "Okay, so 1 of epinephrine is given."
done_well.human_concordance: Matches Human Technical Review: "gave appropriate meds" (Exact timestamp match 01:46)

done_well.category: Shared Mental Model & H's and T's
done_well.title: Collaborative H's & T's Brainstorming & Open Solicitation of Team Opinions
done_well.detail: Leader systematically verbalized reversible causes of PEA (hypoxia from COPD/emphysema, pulmonary embolism/thrombus at @01:59, electrolyte derangements from diarrhea at @02:53, acidosis at @05:51) and actively invited team input, empowering COMPRESSOR to prompt lung auscultation (@03:11) and POC glucose (@04:11).
done_well.evidence_quote: [01:59] TEAM_LEADER: "As far as like H's and T's, she could be hypoxic, she could have any type of clot or thrombus..." → [02:46] AIRWAY_MD: "And she was having diarrhea before." → [02:53] TEAM_LEADER: "Right, so that makes sense for electrolyte derangements... Any other suggestions?"
done_well.human_concordance: Matches Human Review: "verbalized reversible causes of cardiac pea arrest... appreciated leader asking for opinions, they did do a good job of collaborating mentally"

areas_for_improvement.title: Unclosed Communication Loop on Sodium Bicarbonate & Adjuvant Meds
areas_for_improvement.detail: At @05:51, the Team Leader proposed Sodium Bicarbonate as a tentative statement ('We could do an amp of sodium bicarbonate, I'm sure she's got some acidosis going on') and immediately transitioned into a pulse check without issuing a direct order to MED_RN or receiving a verbal readback confirming administration.
areas_for_improvement.actionable_recommendation: Use explicit 3-step directed closed-loop communication for every medication: (1) Leader addresses MED_RN by name/role with drug + dose ('Med RN, give 1 amp Sodium Bicarbonate IV push'), (2) MED_RN repeats back the order, (3) MED_RN announces 'Bicarb 1 amp administered' after flush.
areas_for_improvement.evidence_quote: [05:51 / 351.0s] TEAM_LEADER (utt_019): "We could do an amp of sodium bicarbonate, I'm sure she's got some acidosis going on. It's about 2 minutes, we can check a pulse again. Do we have a pulse?" (Zero MED_RN readback or injection event followed).
areas_for_improvement.human_concordance: Exact Match with Human Reviewer: "no closed loop communication regarding admin of bicarb etc so I could not tell if it was actually given"

areas_for_improvement.title: No Compressor Rotation Across 4m 48s of Continuous Chest Compressions
areas_for_improvement.detail: A single clinician (CLIN-2 in black scrubs) performed manual chest compressions continuously from @01:20 to @06:08 (288s / 4m 48s) across two full 2-minute ACLS cycles without switching compressors during the @03:49–03:55 rhythm check.
areas_for_improvement.actionable_recommendation: Delegate a secondary compressor during initial role assignment (@01:02) and enforce an automatic compressor switch during every 2-minute rhythm/pulse check (@03:49) to prevent rescuers' compression depth decay after 2 minutes.
areas_for_improvement.modality: 3D Spatial Re-ID (CLIN-2) + S1 Optical Flow + S7a (utt_013)
areas_for_improvement.evidence_quote: [03:54 / 234.5s] TEAM_LEADER (utt_013): "Okay, so continue compressions, she's still in PEA" — 3D Spatial Track CLIN-2 remains locked at S1 Sternum ROI continuously from 01:20 to 06:08 without personnel swap.
areas_for_improvement.human_concordance: Exact Match with Human Reviewer: "consider switching out for compressions and delegating differently"

areas_for_improvement.title: Early Epinephrine #2 Dosing Interval (2m 17s vs 3–5 min ACLS Guideline)
areas_for_improvement.detail: Epinephrine #1 was administered at @01:46 and Epinephrine #2 was ordered at @03:54 and confirmed given at @04:03 (interval = 2m 17s / 137s), which is 43 seconds earlier than the AHA ACLS recommended 3–5 minute (180–300s) repeat dosing interval.
areas_for_improvement.actionable_recommendation: Synchronize repeat Epinephrine doses to every second 2-minute pulse check (~4 minutes after first dose) or assign a dedicated medication timer so repeat boluses occur strictly within the 3–5 minute ACLS window.
areas_for_improvement.modality: S7a Diarized ASR (utt_004, utt_014) + Timeline Reducer
areas_for_improvement.evidence_quote: [01:46] Epinephrine #1 administered → [03:54] TEAM_LEADER (utt_013): "We can give another push of epinephrine if it's been 2 minutes" → [04:03] MED_RN (utt_014): "Gave epinephrine" (137s elapsed vs ≥180s target).
areas_for_improvement.human_concordance: Engine Temporal Audit: Quantifies exact 137s dosing interval from spoken readbacks

areas_for_improvement.title: Empiric IV Fluid Bolus Delayed Until Post-ROSC (@06:35) Despite Severe Dehydration Handoff
areas_for_improvement.detail: EMS handoff (@00:00) reported several days of nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and 48 hours of zero PO intake (classic hypovolemic PEA trigger), and AIRWAY_MD highlighted diarrhea at @02:46, but IV fluids (Normal Saline) were not ordered until @06:29–06:35 (27s after ROSC at @06:08).
areas_for_improvement.actionable_recommendation: When H's & T's discussion identifies hypovolemia/GI losses (@02:46), immediately convert that diagnostic finding into an intra-arrest wide-open IV crystalloid bolus order rather than deferring until post-ROSC stabilization.
areas_for_improvement.evidence_quote: [00:00] EMS Handoff (utt_001): "ill with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for several days... past 48 hours unable to eat or drink" → [06:29] TEAM_LEADER (utt_021): "Do we want to give fluids? She's dehydrated most likely" (ordered at 06:35, post-ROSC).
areas_for_improvement.human_concordance: Complements Human H's & T's review with exact pre- vs post-ROSC treatment timing

engine_team_review.human_reviewer: Test Research Team / Trial Run Tabby and Sarah
engine_team_review.human_feedback_narrative: verbalized reversible causes of cardiac pea arrest, gave appropriate meds, no closed loop communication regarding admin of bicarb etc so I could not tell if it was actually given, appreciated leader asking for opinions, consider switching out for compressions and delegating differently
engine_team_review.human_team_comments: Could improve in closed loop communication particularly around administration of meds, it was not clear if certain meds were administered or not. They did do a good job of collaborating mentally, they had clear defined roles and were calm and organized.
